questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman seroconverted for CMV infection during her second pregnancy after a febrile illness in her toddler. Antenatal ultrasound scans were normal. A healthy male infant was delivered at 39 weeks’ gestation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation of the baby to identify congenital CMV infection?

options.text: Serum CMV IgG and avidity assay

questions.explanation: Urine CMV DNA PCR Neonatal serology is unhelpful as this will only reflect transplacental maternal antibody transfer. The mother is already known to be CMV IgG positive. Urine (or saliva) CMV DNA PCR are the recommended first-line investigations in screening for congenital CMV infection as they are more sensitive than plasma CMV DNA PCR, and the clinical specimens are easily obtained. A positive urine/saliva result should be confirmed with a second sample from any site, and plasma CMV DNA PCR, if positive, may be used to monitor the response to treatment. Lumbar puncture would not routinely be performed on a well infant as a screening test for CMV infection, although CSF CMV DNA PCR might be performed as part of the assessment of an infant found to have congenital CMV infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q22

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with HIV , not on therapy, presents to clinic for her first visit. She has had several months of weight loss and intermittent night sweats. She has thrush. She also noted that she has had several weeks of visual changes with “floaters” and blurring of her vision bilaterally. Dilated funduscopic exam was performed, and she was found to have white, perivascular retinal infiltrates and dot-blot hemorrhages.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus CMV is the most common ocular infection in patients living with HIV . It is most common in patients who have CD4 counts <50/μL, and patients often present with complaints of “floaters” and blurred vision. Examination shows necrotizing, full-thickness retinitis, often with some associated hemorrhage, which creates a “brush fire” or “ketchup and cottage cheese” appearance.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q35

needs: Chapter 313 — Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man underwent deceased donor kidney transplant for end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetes mellitus. He received antithymocyte globulin for induction and tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. Investigations: Recipient CMV IgG negative Donor CMV IgG indeterminate
questions.lead_in: What strategy should be recommended to prevent CMV disease?
questions.explanation: Valganciclovir Since the donor had indeterminate CMV serology, and the recipient was CMV seronegative, clinicians should assume that the donor was CMV seropositive since this is the higherrisk possibility and administer prophylaxis accordingly. The standard for CMV D+/R− patients is to administer valganciclovir for 6 months. Valganciclovir is rapidly metabolized to active ganciclovir in the GI tract and liver and may be taken once daily. Use of oral ganciclovir has very low bioavailability and would have a very high pill burden. Foscarnet and cidofovir are only available IV , and their role is for CMV prophylaxis when first-line treatments are contraindicated, or there is resistance. Aciclovir is not active against CMV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q25

questions.question: PCR question about increased sensitivity and differentiating active from latent infection due to viruses.

parts.text: What are 2 clinical indications for the use of EBV PCR to diagnose active infection.
What are 2 clinical indications for the use of CMV PCR to diagnose active infection.

questions.model_answer: a) EBV PCR indications (2): (1) Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) screening/diagnosis in solid organ or HSCT recipients. (2) CNS lymphoma diagnosis in HIV/AIDS patients (EBV DNA in CSF). b) CMV PCR indications (2): (1) Monitoring for CMV reactivation/disease in solid organ and HSCT transplant recipients (preemptive therapy guidance). (2) Diagnosis of CMV end-organ disease (e.g. colitis, retinitis) or congenital CMV infection.

questions.question: 4. You are called in neonatal ICU for evaluation a child suspected of having congenital CMV disease. He has a substantial microcephaly.

parts.text: What is the percentage of infants born with congenital CMV infection?
b) List 3 different ways CMV can be transmitted vertically?
c) List 3 other clinical signs associated with congenital CMV you would look for?
d) What are the 2 most common developmental consequences of congenital CMV infection?
e) List 2 drugs you can use to treat congenital CMV disease.

cohort_answer.text: Incidence: 0.5-1% (Redbook) - most common congenital viral infection. Transmission: Transplacental/intrauterine; During delivery (intrapartum from cervical secretions); Breastfeeding. Clinical signs: jaundice from direct hyperbilirubinemia, petechiae from thrombocytopenia, purpura, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, intracerebral (periventricular) calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, retinitis, developmental delays. Most common developmental consequences: Sensorineural hearing loss (most common); Developmental delay. Drugs: Ganciclovir, Valganciclovir (SE: neutropenia, hepatotoxicity). Neonates with symptomatic congenital CMV disease treated with oral valganciclovir x6mo have improved audiologic/neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2yrs.

questions.question: Case of congenital CMV with microcephaly + calcifications.

parts.text: Percentage of infants affected.
Routes of vertical transmission.
Three physical examination findings other than those above.
Two late developmental issues.
Name two treatments.

cohort_answer.text: Percentage affected: 0.5-1%. Routes of vertical transmission: In utero, intrapartum through infected genital tract secretions, post natal through breast milk. Other PE findings: Petechiae; Jaundice; Hepatosplenomegaly. Late developmental issues: Developmental delay; Sensorineural hearing loss. Treatments: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir

parts.text: CMV. Which of the following would you consider using for treatment given the following mutations? Options: HD ganciclovir, Foscarnet, Cidofovir. Mutations: UL97, UL54.

cohort_answer.text: UL97 mutation - HD ganciclovir: yes; Foscarnet: yes; Cidofovir: yes. UL54 mutation - HD ganciclovir: no; Foscarnet: Yes (not 100% resistant); Cidofovir: no

questions.question: An 18-week pregnant nurse is sent to you for a positive CMV IgM and IgG. She has an 18-months old boy who just started daycare when she resumed working on the pediatric ward.

parts.text: Other than primary infection, list 3 possible interpretations for this serology result.
The test is repeated and the result is the same. What are 3 strategies you can use to differentiate between the possibilities?
What is the risk of transmission to the fetus if this is a primary infection?
What is the risk if the mother has been immune for many years?
What is the greatest epidemiological risk factor for primary infection in this patient?

questions.model_answer: a) Possible interpretations of IgM+/IgG+ other than primary infection (3): (1) Reactivation of latent CMV infection. (2) Reinfection with a different CMV strain. (3) Persistently positive IgM from a remote past infection (IgM can persist/recur for months to years, false positive-like pattern). b) Strategies to differentiate (3): (1) IgG avidity testing (low avidity suggests infection within past 2-4 months; high avidity suggests past/remote infection). (2) Repeat serology in 2-3 weeks looking for rising IgG titers (seroconversion supports primary). (3) Compare with prior banked serology if available to document seroconversion. c) Risk of fetal transmission with primary infection: approximately 30-40% (higher in later pregnancy, but earlier infection carries greater severity). d) Risk with longstanding maternal immunity (non-primary/reactivation): much lower, approximately 1-2%. e) Greatest epidemiologic risk factor: close contact with young children in daycare (toddler's saliva/urine), especially her own young child recently started in daycare.

questions.question: There are established and emerging therapies for CMV. Name the molecular target of each antiviral in the table.

parts.text: Cidofovir
Foscarnet
Maribavir
Letermovir

cohort_answer.text: Letermovir - inhibits CMV terminase complex, encoded by UL 56 & 89 (CMV ppx in BMT pts, less severe disease if receiving this ppx, less myelotoxicity)
cohort_answer.source: MB 2017 (inline after question (partial answer given only for the Letermovir row))

questions.question: 2. Letermovir is a new agent used to treat CMV.

parts.text: What is its target? (1)
What is its mechanism of action? (1)

cohort_answer.text: Target: pUL56 (CMV terminase enzyme complex - UL51, UL56, UL89). Mechanism: Disrupts the viral terminase complex, which is essential for DNA packaging; interferes with pUL56 gene product; complex required for viral DNA processing and packaging; active against most CMV isolates resistant to other antivirals; doesn't need phosphorylation like ganciclovir; doesn't inhibit viral DNA polymerase like ganciclovir/cidofovir/foscarnet; of the herpes viruses only useful for CMV

questions.question:
Q37 (2018)
Woman who is 16 weeks pregnant has fevers and sore throat. At 20 weeks, her IgM and IgG are positive for CMV

parts.text: a) Name one test that would help determine whether this is a primary infection
b) If this is a primary infection, what is the probability her newborn baby will be symptomatic?
c) If the newborn is symptomatic, what is the probability that her newborn will have neurological sequelae?
d) Name two findings in utero that are suggestive of CMV.

cohort_answer.text: Test: IgG avidity testing. Primary infection newborn risk: overall cCMV risk 0.5-5% depending on seroprevalence; primary infection 30% cCMV risk (non-primary 1-2%); of infected, ~10-15% symptomatic. Neurological sequelae if symptomatic: 30%. In utero findings: periventricular calcification, ventriculomegaly, hepatomegaly

questions.question: List 2 disadvantages for the following testing regarding CMV:

parts.text: Culture
Serology IgM/IgG
PCR

questions.model_answer: a) Culture: (1) Slow turnaround (shell vial still takes 1-2 days, conventional culture longer). (2) Lower sensitivity than PCR, especially for blood/plasma viremia; does not reflect viral load well. b) Serology IgM/IgG: (1) Cannot distinguish reactivation/reinfection from primary infection reliably (IgM can persist or reappear). (2) Not useful in immunocompromised hosts who may fail to mount antibody response, and does not indicate active/ongoing replication. c) PCR: (1) Lack of standardization between labs/assays historically (different results across platforms, though improved with WHO international standard). (2) Detects DNA without necessarily indicating clinically significant disease (can be positive with low-level subclinical viremia), cost and access.

questions.question:
Q40 (2018)
Pregnant woman 34 wks GA, CMV symptoms, IgM/IgG+

parts.text: A) What test to do to know if recent infection
B) Risk of symptomatic infection in baby if infected
C) Risk of neurological seq. if infected:
D) Baby born, has some feature of cmv, 1 test to diagnose
E) Risk of symptomatic CMV infection in newborn after primary infection in 1-2 trimester

cohort_answer.text: Test for recent infection: IgG avidity (low avidity means recent infection). Risk of symptomatic infection in baby: Redbook: 10%. Risk of neurological sequelae: 40-60%. Test to diagnose in baby: Detection of CMV PCR in urine, saliva, respiratory tract secretions, blood, or CSF obtained within 3 weeks of birth. Risk of symptomatic CMV infection after primary infection in T1&2: Risk in T1&2 = 30-40% of infection; 10% of infected babies will be symptomatic; Therefore: 0.03-0.04%

questions.question: Infant with suspected congenital CMV based on IUGR and microcephaly

parts.text: Name three physical exam findings of congenital CMV in addition to above.
What are the 2 most important neurodevelopmental impairments from congenital CMV?
What are two treatments for congenital CMV?
What percentage of babies are born with congenital CMV?
What are 3 mechanisms of vertical transmission?

cohort_answer.text: Physical exam findings: Hepatomegaly, Petechiae (thrombocytopenia), Jaundice, Ventriculomegaly, Visual/hearing deficit, Chorioretinitis, SNHL, Seizures. Neurodevelopmental impairments: Learning disability/cognitive impairment (35-50%), Hearing deficits/SNHL (35%) (visual deficits/chorioretinitis 10-15%). Treatments: Ganciclovir, Valganciclovir (Foscarnet/Cidofovir for refractory disease); treat symptomatic congenital CMV, initiate within first 30 days of life. Percentage born with congenital CMV: 0.4-4% of live births (CPS: 0.5-1% developed countries up to 6% developing); if primary infection in pregnancy T1-2: 30-40%, T3: 40-70%. Vertical transmission mechanisms: Transplacental, Breastmilk, Close contact with infant (urine, blood, vaginal secretions)

questions.question: Patient diagnosed with CMV Pneumonia

parts.text: How do you obtain a definitive diagnosis?
Name 2 mutations that confer resistance to ganciclovir and indicate whether or not high dose will overcome it

cohort_answer.text: Definitive diagnosis: clinical symptoms/signs of pneumonia (new infiltrates, hypoxia, tachypnea, dyspnea) combined with CMV documented in lung tissue by virus isolation, rapid culture, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, or DNA hybridization. Mutations: UL54 DNA polymerase mutation (confers resistance to all standard agents - ganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir); UL97 kinase mutation (decreases phosphorylation of GCV; multiple mutations conferring 5-15 fold increased IC50; UL97 arises first, >90%; does not affect foscarnet/cidofovir). UL97 mutants can sometimes be overcome with high dose ganciclovir (only mild disease, specific mutations <5-10 fold increase); otherwise treat with foscarnet/cidofovir. UL54 mutations should use foscarnet

questions.question: PM 8. Lady 18 weeks pregnant who has CMV IgG positive and IgM positive. She has another child who is 18 months old and goes to daycare. She also works in the pediatric inpatient ward. She is now in your office at 20 weeks.

parts.text: What are 3 explanations for her serology other than acute infection (1.5)
What additional tests would you do to sort it out (1)
What is the percentage transmission for first infection? (0.5)
What is the percentage transmission if she was infected a few years ago? (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Explanations: False positive test; IgM serofast; Reactivation of latent infection; Infection with different strain; IVIG. Additional test: CMV IgG avidity testing (should increase in convalescence; repeat IgG looking for 4-fold increase in titre). First infection transmission: 32% (30-40%). Prior infection transmission: 1.4%.

questions.question: Letermovir is a new agent used to prevent CMV infection.

parts.text: What is its target?
What is its mechanism of action?

cohort_answer.text: Target: CMV terminase complex (UL56). Mechanism: Inhibitor of CMV terminase complex, which cleaves the long DNA chain produced during CMV replication into single functional units and packages the genome into capsids needed for new virions; little to no cross-resistance with current anti-CMV drugs

questions.question: List two limitations of each of the following diagnostic methods for CMV infection: Viral culture; IgG/IgM; Nucleic acid testing

parts.text: Viral culture
IgG/IgM
Nucleic acid testing

cohort_answer.text: Viral culture: prolonged processing time, not clinically useful in real time, poor sensitivity, requires viable CMV, not generally used to monitor treatment response due to time requirements. IgG/IgM: not useful for CMV disease diagnosis in transplant due to attenuated/delayed antibody production, not useful for guiding duration of therapy, IVIG alters results, IgM persists for a long time making acute vs non-acute differentiation difficult. Nucleic acid testing: currently no widely accepted viral threshold for predicting CMV disease, lack of assay standardization; highly sensitive, may detect latent CMV, localized disease may not be picked up.

questions.question: Antiviral drugs against Herpesviruses / CMV.

parts.text: Mechanism of action of Ganciclovir
2 mechanisms of resistance to Ganciclovir
Mechanism of action of Foscarnet (pyrophosphate analogs)
Mechanism of action of Acyclovir
Mechanism of action of Letermovir (CMV terminase complex inhibitor)

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir: competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate to inhibit viral DNA polymerase and block viral DNA synthesis; primarily reserved for CMV, also active against HSV-1/2 (same mechanism as valganciclovir). Resistance: UL97 gene mutation (most common, occurs prior to UL54, causes deficiency in viral kinase for ganciclovir phosphorylation/activation, cidofovir and foscarnet usually retain efficacy) and UL54 mutation (often co-exists with UL97, changes viral DNA polymerase, cross-resistance to cidofovir common, cross-resistance to foscarnet rare; HSV isolates resistant to acyclovir due to absent TK are also resistant to ganciclovir). Foscarnet: inorganic pyrophosphate analog, selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase by blocking pyrophosphate binding sites, suppressing viral replication; resistance occurs secondary to some but not all UL54 mutations; primarily reserved for ganciclovir-resistant CMV, also effective against HSV/VZV including acyclovir-resistant isolates; main adverse effect is nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting, minimized with hydration). Acyclovir: synthetic purine nucleoside analog with high affinity for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV thymidine kinase which phosphorylates/activates the drug; human cellular guanylate kinase further phosphorylates it to acyclovir triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA synthesis by competitively inhibiting/inactivating viral DNA polymerase and causing DNA chain termination (valacyclovir, penciclovir, famciclovir have similar mechanisms; cidofovir similar but does not require viral TK). Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (novel mechanism), which normally cleaves long DNA chains produced during CMV replication into single functional units; only active against CMV; FDA approved for CMV prophylaxis in adult CMV-seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients; low barrier to resistance in vitro; no dosage adjustment needed with CrCl >10 mL/min.

parts.text: CMV. What is the mechanism of action of ganciclovir, foscarnet, and letermovir? What are two gene mutations for ganciclovir and the location in the cell impacted?

questions.model_answer: Mechanisms of action: Ganciclovir - a guanosine nucleoside analogue that is first phosphorylated by the CMV-encoded UL97 protein kinase (and then by cellular kinases) to its active triphosphate form, which competitively inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) and causes chain termination. Foscarnet - a pyrophosphate analogue that directly (without requiring intracellular phosphorylation) binds the pyrophosphate-binding site of the viral DNA polymerase, blocking cleavage of pyrophosphate from nucleoside triphosphates and inhibiting DNA chain elongation. Letermovir - inhibits the CMV terminase complex (pUL56/pUL89/pUL51), blocking viral DNA cleavage and packaging into capsids (does not inhibit the DNA polymerase). Two gene mutations for ganciclovir resistance and their cellular impact: (1) UL97 mutation - affects the viral kinase responsible for the initial phosphorylation step of ganciclovir (cytoplasmic activation step, most common cause of resistance, low-to-moderate level); (2) UL54 mutation - affects the viral DNA polymerase itself (the ultimate drug target), causing higher-level resistance and potential cross-resistance to cidofovir and/or foscarnet depending on mutation location.

parts.text: Given a Table. Fill in 2 most common mutations for CMV resistance, whether or not you would use the below therapy in the setting of the named mutation. Columns: Mutation, High dose Gancyclovir, Foscarnet, Cidofovir. Rows: 1. 2.

questions.model_answer: Two most common CMV resistance mutations: (1) UL97 mutation - confers resistance to ganciclovir (reduced viral kinase-mediated phosphorylation); high-dose ganciclovir may still be tried for low-grade mutations but is often inadequate; foscarnet - still active (does not require UL97 phosphorylation), can use; cidofovir - still active (activated by cellular, not viral, kinases), can use. (2) UL54 (DNA polymerase) mutation - confers resistance to ganciclovir; high-dose ganciclovir - generally not effective; foscarnet - variable, some UL54 mutations retain foscarnet susceptibility, others confer cross-resistance (use with caution/confirm susceptibility); cidofovir - often cross-resistant (shares the polymerase target), generally avoid unless susceptibility confirmed.

parts.text: Asked for target for site of action if ganciclovir, foscarnet and Maribavir

questions.model_answer: Site of action: Ganciclovir - viral DNA polymerase (UL54), after activation via phosphorylation by the UL97 kinase. Foscarnet - viral DNA polymerase (UL54), acting directly at the pyrophosphate-binding site without requiring phosphorylation. Maribavir - the viral UL97 protein kinase itself, which it inhibits directly, blocking downstream viral DNA synthesis, capsid nuclear egress, and CMV gene expression.

questions.question: Young woman from Peru is pregnant. Her son is in daycare. She is a pediatrician. She has IgG and IgM positive CMV serology

parts.text: what are three ways to interpret this other than acute infection?
What 3 additional tests would you order to clarify?

What is her risk of transmitting if she were IgG positive for several years?

cohort_answer.text: A) False positive serology; remote infection (IgM can remain positive up to 18 months); woman received IVIG. B) IgG avidity; amniotic fluid CMV PCR; fetal US. C) 40% overall if primary infection. D) 1-2%, however likely an underestimate.

questions.question: CMV drugs.

parts.text: What is the MOA of valganciclovir, foscarnet, and letermovir?
Give two mutations for CMV for ganciclovir resistance and their viral targets.

questions.model_answer: a) MOA: Valganciclovir (prodrug of ganciclovir) - phosphorylated by viral UL97 kinase then host kinases to triphosphate form, competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase (UL54) and causes chain termination. Foscarnet - pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase without requiring phosphorylation. Letermovir - inhibits the HCMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56/UL89), blocking viral DNA cleavage/packaging (not a polymerase inhibitor). b) Ganciclovir resistance mutations (2) and viral targets: (1) UL97 mutation - reduces phosphorylation/activation of ganciclovir (kinase target). (2) UL54 mutation - alters viral DNA polymerase itself, reduces ganciclovir binding (and can confer cross-resistance to cidofovir/foscarnet depending on mutation).

questions.question: CMV Refractory to Ganciclovir

parts.text: What are 2 genes that when mutated can lead to ganciclovir resistance?
What are 2 alternative antivirals that can be used in ganciclovir-refractory CMV?

questions.model_answer: a) Two genes with mutations causing ganciclovir resistance: UL97 (viral kinase, reduces GCV phosphorylation) and UL54 (viral DNA polymerase, reduces GCV binding). b) Two alternative antivirals for ganciclovir-refractory CMV: foscarnet and cidofovir (maribavir also acceptable as newer alternative).

questions.question: G1P2 patient who is 22 weeks pregnant. Serology revealed IgM+, IgG+. These were checked in the context of IUGR.

parts.text: Which test can you do to determine the timing of acquisition
Risk of vertical transmission in this patient assuming primary CMV infection.
What is the gold standard test for diagnosing congenital CMV in newborn and what is the timing of the test?

questions.model_answer: a) Test to determine timing of acquisition: IgG avidity testing (low avidity suggests infection within the preceding 2-4 months). b) Risk of vertical transmission with primary CMV infection: approximately 30-40%. c) Gold standard test for congenital CMV in the newborn: urine (or saliva) CMV PCR/viral culture, performed within the first 3 weeks (ideally 21 days) of life to distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection.

questions.question: Q80 2023 Day 2. CMV case with treatment failure on ganciclovir, details not relevant to questions. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: 2 resistance mechanisms for ganciclovir resistance (just the genes)
2 drugs to treat ganciclovir resistant CMV

cohort_answer.text:
2 resistance mechanisms: UL97 - reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation caused by mutations or deletion in the phosphotransferase (encoded by UL97). UL54 - altered viral DNA polymerase (encoded by UL54).
2 drugs: Cidofovir (dCTP analogue binding viral DNA polymerase UL54; ok for UL97, may not work for UL54); Foscarnet (inhibits viral DNA polymerase at PPi site UL54; ok for UL97, may not work for UL54); Letermovir (prophylaxis only; inhibits CMV replication by binding viral terminase complex UL51/UL56/both; ok for UL97 or UL54 mutation); Maribavir (inhibits phosphorylation of several viral proteins e.g. UL44, inhibits UL97; ok for UL97 or UL54 mutation).

questions.question: Q35 (2023, PM) - Incomplete??? Unclear what virus they are talking about. Pregnant woman with CMV at 22 weeks. (PREGNANCY)

parts.text: Gold standard
Risk of vertical transmission from primary infection during pregnancy

questions.model_answer: a) Gold standard for diagnosing congenital CMV: newborn urine (or saliva) PCR/culture within the first 21 days of life. b) Risk of vertical transmission with primary maternal infection: approximately 30-40%. c) To help determine timing of infection: IgG avidity testing (low avidity = recent infection within 2-4 months).

questions.question: Child has CMV pneumonia, pregnant nurse asks about potential precautions.

parts.text: A. What measures (if any) to take for nurse?

cohort_answer.text: Routine practices. Wear gloves if HCW expects contact with body secretions/excretions and practice hand hygiene after glove removal. Avoid kissing or cuddling infants/young children. HCW who are pregnant can be relocated to a different patient. Serology not recommended as seropositive pregnant women still at risk

questions.question: Q28 (2017 PM). Asked for target site of action for ganciclovir, foscarnet, and maribavir

parts.text: State target site of action for each CMV drug

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir - inhibits viral DNA polymerase UL54 (via dNTP binding site/catalytic site). Foscarnet - inhibits viral DNA polymerase UL54 (via pyrophosphate binding site). Maribavir - inhibits viral UL97 kinase, preventing nuclear egress. UL97 mutations confer resistance to ganciclovir/valganciclovir; UL54 mutation confers multidrug resistance.

questions.question: Q29 (2018). Letermovir is a new agent used to treat CMV

parts.text: a) What is its target?
b) What is the MOA?

cohort_answer.text: Target: UL56 (component of CMV terminase enzyme complex). MOA: terminase complex catalyzes cleavage and packaging of viral DNA; letermovir inhibits CMV replication by blocking cleavage/packaging; active against most CMV isolates resistant to other antivirals; doesn't need phosphorylation like ganciclovir; doesn't inhibit viral DNA polymerase like ganciclovir/cidofovir/foscarnet; only active against CMV.

B) Risk to fetus

questions.question:
Q38 (2012 PM)
CMV

parts.text: A. 2 strategies for post-transplant/BMT

cohort_answer.text:
Universal ppx - treat all pts regardless of risk group. Pro: easy to implement, prevents reactivation of other herpes viruses. Con: toxicity, cost.
Pre-emptive approach - Test CMV VL qweekly from day 10-100 and start tx as soon as detectable; more often for moderate to low risk. Adv: limited toxicity, lower resistance, lower cost. Disadv: pt compliance, more bloodwork, prevents disease not infection.
Hybrid approach - Shorter course of ppx followed by pre-emptive approach qweekly x 8-12 wks

parts.text: A. Give three reasons to use the CMV antigenemia or PCR assay

cohort_answer.text:
CMV Antigenemia Assay: rapidly and directly detects CMV proteins (pp65) in peripheral blood WBC - detects labeled monoclonal Ab specific to pp65 lower matrix protein of CMV. High specificity. Can be done in BAL, blood and tissue samples. Results available within 24h. Antigenemia correlates with viremia in HIV infected pts and recipients of SOT. LIMITATIONS: lack of stability of whole blood specimen, lack of standardization, subjective interpretation, need for sufficient neutrophil numbers (can't do in neutropenia), rather less sensitive in neutropenia, sample processing required within 6-8 hours of collection, labor intensive, unable to detect free virus in fluids.
CMV PCR Assay: High sensitivity. Can use for diagnosing active CMV, monitoring response to therapy. Tissue specific PCR is useful. Sterile fluid PCR is useful (eg vitreous fluid). Can use plasma or whole blood specimens - VL higher and DNA more frequently detected in whole blood than in plasma; low levels of CMV DNA do not always correlate with CMV disease. CMV DNA is stable in whole blood and plasma for up to 5d when stored at 4 degrees C. There are still variabilities between different assays used, even though WHO developed a 'standardization' in 2010, therefore hard to have a hard cutoff

questions.question: List 2 limitations for the following testing regarding CMV: Viral Culture; CMV IgM and IgG; PCR/Nucleic Acid Test

parts.text: Viral Culture
CMV IgM and IgG
PCR/Nucleic Acid Test

cohort_answer.text: Viral Culture: Grows slowly (1-6 weeks); Lacks sensitivity particularly blood; useful in congenital CMV - urine and tissue. CMV IgM and IgG: Requirement for paired serum samples limits utility of timely diagnosis; IgM may persist for several months so stand-alone may provide misleading information (may represent prior infection rather than current). PCR/NAT: Cannot distinguish between active latent and actively replicating virus; unable to differentiate low-level from high-level replication (need quantitative PCR); despite WHO international standard units, there is still variability in viral load values

questions.question: For CMV: Name the mechanisms of: Ganciclovir, Letermovir, Foscarnet, Maribavir. What are 2 resistance mutations for CMV to antivirals. What is the mutation and the target site affected?

parts.text: Mechanism of Ganciclovir
Mechanism of Letermovir
Mechanism of Foscarnet
Mechanism of Maribavir
2 resistance mutations for CMV to antivirals and target site affected

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir - binds UL54 catalytic site of DNA polymerase. Letermovir - binds UL89/56/51 DNA terminase complex, inhibits viral maturation. Foscarnet - binds UL54 DNA polymerase pyrophosphate site. Maribavir - pUL97 kinase inhibitor. Resistance mutations: point mutations in viral DNA polymerase (UL54 gene) - may cause resistance to ganciclovir/foscarnet/cidofovir (some knock out all three); reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation from point mutations/deletions in phosphotransferase encoded by UL97 gene (susceptible to foscarnet/cidofovir).

questions.question: For CMV:

parts.text: Name the mechanisms of Ganciclovir, Letermovir, Foscarnet, Maribavir.
2 resistance mutations for CMV to antivirals. What is the mutation gene and the target site affected?

cohort_answer.text:
Ganciclovir - binds UL54 catalytic site of DNA polymerase causing cessation of DNA chain elongation (after phosphorylation by UL97 kinase). Letermovir - binds UL51/56 DNA terminase complex enzyme, inhibits viral maturation by preventing cleavage into functional units. Foscarnet - binds the UL54 DNA pol pyrophosphate site suppressing viral replication. Maribavir - pUL97 kinase inhibitor (antagonizes ganciclovir).
Resistance mutations: Reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation caused by point mutations or deletions in the phosphotransferase (kinase) encoded by the UL97 gene (resistant to ganciclovir, susceptible to foscarnet and cidofovir). Point mutations in viral DNA polymerase UL54 gene result in resistance to ganciclovir and cidofovir, usually still susceptible to foscarnet.

questions.question: 6. 60F something lady (CMV +) who received her husband's kidney (also CMV +) for polycystic kidney disease.

parts.text: Given her intermediate risk, list 2 acceptable management strategies to reduce her risk of CMV disease.
b) Give 1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each modality

c) She comes back with fever, thrombocytopenia and diarrhea. Her CMV viral load is 56 000 copies/mL. A colon biopsy reveals CMV intracellular inclusions. List 2 drugs you can use as first line treatment for her condition.
d) For how long will you treat her?

cohort_answer.text: Strategies: 1. Preemptive therapy (weekly CMV blood PCR, treat if positive before symptoms/disease develop); 2. Prophylaxis with PO valganciclovir x3mos post transplant. Advantage/disadvantage: Preemptive therapy -> advantage: less likely to develop late disease, eliminate SE of anti-viral medication; disadvantage: requires diligent follow-up and risk of CMV disease developing. Prophylaxis -> advantage: proven to reduce CMV and other opportunistic infections and decreases risk of transplant rejection; disadvantage: SE of medication, cost, risk of developing CMV disease resistant to valganciclovir. First line for CMV colitis: IV ganciclovir, PO valganciclovir. Alternatives (2nd line): IV foscarnet. NB. Cidofovir has never been studied for CMV colitis. Duration: IV ganciclovir (or PO valganciclovir 900mg BID), minimum 2 weeks, generally 2-4 weeks, treat until clearance of viremia and no symptoms.

questions.question: CMV in transplant

parts.text: list and describe two methods for managing potential CMV infections.
What are two options for prophylaxis?

questions.model_answer: a) Two management strategies: (1) Universal prophylaxis - give antiviral (e.g. valganciclovir or letermovir) to all at-risk patients starting early post-transplant for a defined duration, regardless of CMV PCR status, to prevent reactivation. (2) Preemptive therapy - serial CMV PCR monitoring post-transplant, treating only when viremia is first detected above a threshold, before symptomatic disease develops. b) Prophylaxis options: (1) Valganciclovir (oral, standard first-line). (2) Letermovir (HSCT, terminase inhibitor, no myelosuppression - preferred in high-risk HSCT given lack of marrow toxicity).

questions.model_answer: Congenital infection associations: Osteitis - congenital syphilis (also rubella causing metaphyseal lucencies). questions.question: You see a patient who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant 1 month ago. He is found to have a positive CMV PCR.

parts.text: List FIVE risk factors for CMV infection in hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Describe prophylactic therapy and pre-emptive therapy.
How is ganciclovir cleared and in what population is dose adjustment required?
List THREE alternate medications that can be used with mutations in UL97 and ONE alternate medication that can be used with mutations in UL54.

questions.model_answer: a) Five risk factors for CMV in HSCT: (1) CMV-seropositive recipient (D+/R+ or D-/R+ - recipient seropositivity is main driver of reactivation). (2) Donor/recipient CMV serostatus mismatch (D+/R-). (3) Type of transplant - allogeneic (especially mismatched/unrelated donor or cord blood) higher risk than autologous. (4) Graft-versus-host disease and its immunosuppressive treatment. (5) T-cell depletion (in vivo, e.g. ATG/alemtuzumab, or ex vivo graft manipulation). b) Prophylactic therapy: antiviral (letermovir preferred in HSCT, or valganciclovir) given to all at-risk patients from early post-transplant through a defined high-risk period regardless of PCR status. Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative CMV PCR monitoring, initiating treatment (valganciclovir/ganciclovir) only once viremia is detected above a defined threshold, before end-organ disease develops. c) Ganciclovir clearance: renally cleared, excreted largely unchanged in urine; dose adjustment required in renal impairment (reduced eGFR). d) UL97 mutation alternatives (3): foscarnet, cidofovir, maribavir. UL54 mutation alternative (1): foscarnet (cidofovir may retain some activity depending on specific mutation, but foscarnet is the standard alternative).

questions.question: CMV in renal transplant patient (CMV D+/R+), patient has fever and colitis. WBC 3.4, Cr 126.

parts.text: 2 possible CMV prevention strategies
1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each
CMV PCR 56000, fever, colitis. 2 first-line treatments in this patient, and duration of tx?

cohort_answer.text: A) Pre-emptive therapy (monitor CMV VL qweekly x12 weeks, treat if viremic); prophylaxis. B) Pre-emptive: advantage - effective agents also treat CMV disease, lower cost; disadvantage - frequent weekly bloodwork, agents myelosuppressive/nephrotoxic. Letermovir ppx: advantage - less myelo/nephrotoxic, lower rates of invasive CMV infection vs placebo; disadvantage - cost of daily tx, need to rule out active CMV disease (switch regimen), associated with late onset CMV disease. C) First line: IV Ganciclovir 5mg/kg q12h for severe/life-threatening disease, high VL or questionable oral absorption; PO Valganciclovir 900mg BID for mild-moderate disease. Duration until resolution of clinical symptoms and viral load undetectable, minimum 2 weeks; secondary ppx 1-3 months may be considered; caution reduction in immunosuppression especially if mod-severe disease.

questions.question: Post HSCT and develops CMV DNAemia.

parts.text: What are 5 risk factors for CMV disease
Define pre-emptive and prophylaxis strategies (no advantages/disadvantages, just describe)
How is IV ganciclovir metabolized, and when might the dose need adjusting
For resistant CMV disease, name three antivirals that may be considered for UL97 mutation and one for UL54 mutation.

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: CMV seropositivity (D-/R+); T cell depletion (ATG); GVHD; Immunosuppressive drugs (steroids, alemtuzumab); Lymphopenia. Pre-emptive therapy: Patients monitored frequently (weekly) with CMV load and antiviral therapy initiated when viral replication reaches a certain assay threshold defined at each institution. Prophylaxis: Immediate start of prophylaxis (ganciclovir, valganciclovir, letermovir) post-transplant in high risk patients. Ganciclovir metabolism: Acyclic analog of nucleoside guanosine, converted intracellularly to ganciclovir 5'-monophosphate by viral kinase encoded by CMV gene UL97 during infection; cellular kinases catalyze formation of ganciclovir diphosphate and triphosphate (10-fold greater concentration in CMV infected cells); ganciclovir triphosphate is a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation into DNA, preferentially inhibiting viral DNA polymerases, and is a poor substrate for chain elongation, disrupting viral DNA synthesis. Dose adjustment needed: Renal impairment; Dialysis; Pre-emptive therapy (induction 5mg/kg q12 vs maintenance 5mg/kg q24); UL97 mutation for <5x (10mg/kg q12, off-label); Intravitreal injection (off-label). Resistant CMV: UL97 mutation - Foscarnet, Cidofovir, Maribavir, possibly high dose ganciclovir. UL54 mutation - Maribavir, Foscarnet (avoid cidofovir)
